4. Host‑Based Firewall — Firewalld

Source: CIS AlmaLinux OS 10 Benchmark v1.0.0, Section 4.1

The target system uses firewalld with the nftables backend (README Part 18.1). The recommendations in this section are taken directly from the CIS AlmaLinux OS 10 Benchmark, which provides native firewalld‑specific audit and remediation procedures. On Gentoo, firewalld uses nftables as its default backend; unlike RPM‑based distributions, no additional backend configuration is required beyond the FirewallBackend setting in /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf.

The AlmaLinux benchmark is organised as follows: - 4.1.1 — Ensure firewalld is installed. - 4.1.2 — Ensure the firewalld backend is configured (must be nftables). - 4.1.3 — Ensure firewalld.service is running and enabled. - 4.1.4 — Ensure the active zone target is not set to ACCEPT and that the target is written as a permanent rule. - 4.1.5 — Ensure loopback traffic is configured (the lo interface must be in a zone with target ACCEPT). - 4.1.6 — Ensure anti‑spoofing rich rules are configured for loopback source addresses. - 4.1.7 — Ensure only approved services and ports are permitted.

Each subsection below reproduces the AlmaLinux benchmark’s audit procedure (adapted for Gentoo’s filesystem layout and command conventions) and its remediation procedure.

4.1.1 Ensure firewalld is installed (Automated)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required The firewalld package must be installed. firewalld provides a dynamically managed firewall with support for network/firewall zones that define the trust level of network connections or interfaces. It acts as a front‑end for the Linux kernel’s netfilter framework via the nftables userspace utility.

Gentoo Implementation net-firewall/firewalld is emerged and active (README Part 18.1). The package is installed from the Gentoo main repository.

Audit

qpkg -I firewalld && echo "✅ firewalld installed" || echo "❌ firewalld NOT installed"

If the command returns nothing (package not installed), the audit fails.

Remediation

emerge --ask net-firewall/firewalld

4.1.2 Ensure firewalld backend is configured (Automated)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required The FirewallBackend parameter in /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf must be set to nftables. The iptables backend is deprecated and should not be used. On Gentoo, nftables is the default and only supported backend for modern firewalld deployments.

Gentoo Implementation The configuration file already contains FirewallBackend=nftables (README Part 18.1). This is the default setting on Gentoo and on any modern firewalld installation.

Audit

grep -Psi -- '^\h*FirewallBackend\h*=\h*nftables\b' /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf

The command must return a matching line showing FirewallBackend=nftables. If it returns nothing, or if the line is commented out or set to a different value, the audit fails.

Remediation

# If the line exists but has a different value:
sed -i 's/^FirewallBackend=.*/FirewallBackend=nftables/' /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf
# If the line does not exist:
echo "FirewallBackend=nftables" >> /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf
firewall-cmd --reload

4.1.3 Ensure firewalld.service is configured (Automated)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required firewalld.service must be enabled to start automatically at boot and must currently be active. The firewall rules configured through FirewallD are only enforced when the service is running.

Gentoo Implementation firewalld.service is enabled and active (README Part 18.1).

Audit

systemctl is-enabled firewalld.service
# Must output: enabled
systemctl is-active firewalld.service
# Must output: active

If either command returns anything other than enabled or active respectively, the audit fails.

Remediation

systemctl unmask firewalld.service 2>/dev/null || true
systemctl enable --now firewalld.service

4.1.4 Ensure firewalld active zone target is configured (Automated)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required For every active zone except those containing only the loopback interface (lo), the zone target must not be set to ACCEPT. Additionally, the target must be written as a permanent rule (i.e., committed with --permanent) so that it survives a daemon reload or system reboot. This implements a “deny by default, allow by exception” policy: any traffic not explicitly permitted by a service, port, or rich rule is dropped or rejected.

The AlmaLinux benchmark notes that the target may be set to DROP, REJECT, or default. The default target provides a convenient way to implement a deny‑by‑default policy while still allowing essential ICMP traffic (such as neighbour discovery and router advertisements).

Gentoo Implementation The default zone is drop, and the active interfaces (Ethernet) are assigned to the drop zone. The loopback interface is in the trusted zone, which has target ACCEPT — this is explicitly permitted by the AlmaLinux benchmark (see 4.1.5). All zone assignments are permanent.

The audit script from the AlmaLinux benchmark has been adapted below to run on Gentoo. It performs the following checks: 1. Iterates over all active zones. 2. Excludes zones whose only interface is lo or virtual interfaces (virbr*). 3. For each remaining zone, extracts the running target and the permanent target. 4. If the running target is unset or ACCEPT, the zone fails. 5. If the running target does not match the permanent target, the zone fails (the rule is not permanent).

Audit

#!/bin/bash
# Adapted from CIS AlmaLinux OS 10 Benchmark §4.1.4
a_output=(); a_output2=()
while IFS= read -r l_zone; do
    l_zone="$(awk -F'(' '{print $1}' <<< "${l_zone// /}")"
    l_interfaces="$(firewall-cmd --zone="$l_zone" --list-interfaces)"
    # Exclude loopback and virtual interfaces from the ACCEPT check
    if ! grep -Psq -- '^(lo|virbr[^\h]+)\h*$' <<< "${l_interfaces/ /}"; then
        l_ptarget="$(firewall-cmd --permanent --zone="$l_zone" --get-target)"
        l_target="$(cut -d: -f2 <<< "$(grep -Pso -- '^\h*target:\h+\H+\b' \
                   <<< "$(firewall-cmd --list-all --zone="$l_zone")")" | xargs)"
        if [ -z "$l_target" ] || [ "${l_target,,}" = "accept" ]; then
            a_output2+=(" - Active zone: \"$l_zone\"" \
                        " Target is: \"$l_target\" for interfaces: \"$l_interfaces\"")
        elif [ ! "${l_target,,}" = "${l_ptarget,,}" ]; then
            a_output2+=(" - Active zone: \"$l_zone\"" \
                        " Target is: \"$l_target\" is not a permanent firewall rule")
        else
            a_output+=(" - Active zone: \"$l_zone\"" \
                        " Target is: \"$l_target\" for interfaces: \"$l_interfaces\"")
        fi
    fi
done < <(firewall-cmd --get-active-zones | awk '$1!~/interface/{print}')
if [ "${#a_output2[@]}" -gt 0 ]; then
    printf '%s\n' "" "${a_output2[@]}" ""
    echo "❌ Some zones have an incorrect or non‑permanent target"
else
    echo "✅ All active zones have a valid, permanent target set"
fi

No lines should be printed by the a_output2 array. If a_output2 is empty, the system is compliant.

Remediation

# Set the target for a specific zone and make it permanent.
# Replace <ZONE> with the zone name (e.g., 'drop', 'public') and
# <TARGET> with the desired target (DROP, REJECT, or default).
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=<ZONE> --set-target=<TARGET>
firewall-cmd --reload

# Example: set the 'drop' zone to DROP
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=drop --set-target=DROP
firewall-cmd --reload

4.1.5 Ensure firewalld loopback traffic is configured (Manual)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required Loopback traffic (communications between processes on the same machine) must be permitted. The loopback interface (lo) must be assigned to a zone whose target is ACCEPT. If the loopback interface is not assigned to any zone (the output of firewall-cmd --get-zone-of-interface=lo is no zone), the audit fails immediately.

The AlmaLinux benchmark requires two checks: 1. Verify that lo is assigned to a zone (not no zone). 2. Verify that the assigned zone’s target is ACCEPT.

Gentoo Implementation The lo interface is in the trusted zone, which has the target ACCEPT (README Part 18.1). This is consistent with the AlmaLinux benchmark’s expectation that loopback traffic should not be restricted.

Audit

# Step 1: Verify that lo is assigned to a zone
ZONE=$(firewall-cmd --get-zone-of-interface=lo)
if [ "$ZONE" = "no zone" ]; then
    echo "❌ lo is not assigned to any zone"
    exit 1
fi
echo "lo is in zone: $ZONE"

# Step 2: Verify that the zone's target is ACCEPT
firewall-cmd --list-all --zone="$ZONE" | grep -Psi -- '^\h*target:\h+\H+'
# The output must show "target: ACCEPT"

Both steps must succeed. If the target is anything other than ACCEPT, or if lo is not assigned to a zone, the audit fails.

Remediation If the loopback interface is not already assigned to a zone:

firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-interface=lo

If it is in a different zone and needs to be moved:

firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --change-interface=lo

Then reload the firewall to apply the change immediately:

firewall-cmd --reload

4.1.6 Ensure firewalld loopback source address traffic is configured (Manual)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required Rich rules must be present that drop any traffic from a loopback source address (127.0.0.1 or ::1) that is not also destined to a loopback address. This is an anti‑spoofing measure: the loopback interface is the only place where loopback network traffic should appear; all other interfaces should ignore traffic with these source addresses.

The AlmaLinux benchmark requires that the following two rich rules be present on the zone that contains the lo interface: - rule family="ipv4" source address="127.0.0.1" destination NOT address="127.0.0.1" drop - rule family="ipv6" source address="::1" destination NOT address="::1" drop

Gentoo Implementation These rich rules are already configured on the trusted zone (README Part 18.1).

Audit

#!/bin/bash
# Adapted from CIS AlmaLinux OS 10 Benchmark §4.1.6
while IFS= read -r l_zone; do
    echo " - Zone: $l_zone"
    firewall-cmd --zone="$l_zone" --list-rich-rules | \
      grep -P -- '(::1|127\.0\.0\.1)\b'
done < <(firewall-cmd --get-zone-of-interface=lo | xargs)

Expected output (example):

 - Zone: trusted
rule family="ipv4" source address="127.0.0.1" destination NOT address="127.0.0.1" drop
rule family="ipv6" source address="::1" destination NOT address="::1" drop

Both rules (one for IPv4, one for IPv6) must be present. If either rule is missing, the audit fails.

Remediation If the rules are missing, add them to the zone that contains the loopback interface. The AlmaLinux benchmark provides the following commands (adapted for Gentoo):

# Determine the zone that contains lo
LO_ZONE=$(firewall-cmd --get-zone-of-interface=lo)

# Add the IPv4 anti‑spoofing rule
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone="$LO_ZONE" --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address="127.0.0.1" destination not address="127.0.0.1" drop'

# Add the IPv6 anti‑spoofing rule
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone="$LO_ZONE" --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv6 source address="::1" destination not address="::1" drop'

# Reload to apply
firewall-cmd --reload

4.1.7 Ensure firewalld services and ports are configured (Manual)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ⚠️ NEEDS REVIEW (site‑specific)

What’s Required The services and ports permitted in each active firewall zone must be reviewed against site policy. Every allowed service or port should have a documented business need. The default zone target (DROP or REJECT, as configured in 4.1.4) ensures that all traffic not explicitly permitted is denied.

The AlmaLinux benchmark notes that the command firewall-cmd --get-services | tr ' ' '\n' | column can be used to list all services that firewalld recognises by name.

Gentoo Implementation The user’s firewalld configuration (README Part 18.1) allows the following services and ports in the drop zone: - SSH on port 2222 (TCP) - DNS over TLS on port 853 (TCP) - HTTPS on port 443 (TCP and UDP) - Cockpit on port 9090 (TCP, restricted to 127.0.0.1 only)

All other inbound traffic is dropped by the zone’s default DROP target. The administrator must verify that this list conforms to local site policy.

Audit

# List the services and open ports for the active zone(s)
firewall-cmd --list-all --zone="$(firewall-cmd --list-all | awk '/(active)/ { print $1 }')" | \
  grep -P -- '^\h*(services:|ports:)'

# Also review rich rules (which may open additional ports)
firewall-cmd --list-rich-rules

Review the output. Every service and port listed should have a documented justification. Any service or port that is not required should be removed.

Remediation Remove an unnecessary service:

firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-service=<service>

Remove an unnecessary port:

firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-port=<port-number>/<port-type>
# Example: firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-port=25/tcp

Make the running configuration permanent and reload:

firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent
firewall-cmd --reload

5. Access Control

5.1 Configure SSH Server

Secure Shell (SSH) is the primary remote administration protocol on the target system. The SSH daemon configuration (README Part 19.7) satisfies or exceeds every CIS Level 1 SSH recommendation. The SSH client configuration (README Part 19.5) applies matching hardening on the client side. Both configurations are reproduced in full below, with individual audit commands for each parameter.

The OpenSSH daemon reads its configuration from /etc/ssh/sshd_config and from files in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf (via the Include directive). On Gentoo, the system‑wide crypto policy is applied through direct configuration in sshd_config rather than through a separate crypto‑policies framework. The apparmor.d project ships a mature sshd profile that should be loaded in enforce mode.

5.1.1 Ensure permissions on /etc/ssh/sshd_config are configured

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required The file /etc/ssh/sshd_config and any files in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ ending in .conf must be owned by root:root and have mode 0600 or more restrictive.

Audit

stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
# Must show: 600 root:root
find /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d -type f -name '*.conf' -exec stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' {} \;
# All files must show 600 root:root (or more restrictive)

Remediation

chown root:root /etc/ssh/sshd_config
chmod 600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config
find /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d -type f -name '*.conf' -exec chown root:root {} \;
find /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d -type f -name '*.conf' -exec chmod 600 {} \;

5.1.2 – 5.1.3 Ensure permissions on SSH host key files are configured

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required Private SSH host key files must be owned by root:root (or root:ssh_keys on Fedora‑derived distributions) and have mode 0600 or 0640 depending on the group owner. Public SSH host key files must be owned by root:root and have mode 0644 or more restrictive.

Gentoo Implementation On Gentoo, the ssh_keys group does not exist. Private keys are owned by root:root with mode 0600. Public keys are owned by root:root with mode 0644.

Audit

# Private keys
find /etc/ssh -type f -name 'ssh_host_*_key' ! -name '*.pub' -exec stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' {} \;
# Public keys
find /etc/ssh -type f -name 'ssh_host_*_key.pub' -exec stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' {} \;

Remediation

find /etc/ssh -type f -name 'ssh_host_*_key' ! -name '*.pub' -exec chown root:root {} \; -exec chmod 600 {} \;
find /etc/ssh -type f -name 'ssh_host_*_key.pub' -exec chown root:root {} \; -exec chmod 644 {} \;

5.1.4 Ensure sshd access is configured

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required At leastAct as an expert Linux kernel developer and veteran Gentoo system administrator who specializes in security, hardened configurations, and system optimization.

Your Objective: I am building a hardened Gentoo system using the sys-kernel/cachyos-sources from the CachyOS-kernels Gentoo overlay. I need you to thoroughly review my current minimal kernel configuration.

Please analyze the provided minimal-config.txt and cross-reference it with the provided README.md instructions, as well as general Gentoo Hardened Wiki best practices.

Please provide your analysis in the following structured format: 1. Compliance with README: Identify any discrepancies or missing configurations based on the instructions in my README file. 2. Hardening & Security Check: Evaluate the config against standard Gentoo hardened wiki guidelines. Highlight any missing security features or enabled features that introduce vulnerabilities. 3. Minimalism & Debloating: Point out any unnecessary drivers, subsystems, or bloat that can be safely disabled to keep the kernel strictly minimal. 4. CachyOS Specifics: Note any misconfigurations or missed optimization opportunities specifically relevant to CachyOS kernels. 5. Actionable Recommendations: Provide the specific CONFIG_...=y/n/m lines I need to change. one of AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, or DenyGroups must be configured to restrict which users or groups can authenticate via SSH.

Gentoo Implementation AllowGroups sshusers is set in /etc/ssh/sshd_config (README Part 19.7). Only members of the sshusers group may authenticate.

Audit

sshd -T | grep -Pi '^\h*(allow|deny)(users|groups)\h+\H+'
# Must show at least one configured restriction

Remediation

groupadd -f sshusers
usermod -aG sshusers <username>
# Ensure the sshd_config contains:
# AllowGroups sshusers

5.1.5 Ensure sshd Banner is configured

STIG: UBTU‑24‑200640 (CAT II)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation · STIG CAT II | Status: ⚠️ NEEDS REVIEW (STIG banner content)

What’s Required The Banner directive must point to a file whose contents are displayed to the remote user before authentication is permitted. The STIG requires the exact DoD‑mandated banner text.

Gentoo Implementation Banner /etc/ssh/banner is configured. The banner content must be reviewed for STIG compliance (see §1.6).

Audit

sshd -T | grep -i '^banner '
# Must output a path, e.g., banner /etc/ssh/banner
cat "$(sshd -T | awk '/^banner / {print $2}')"

Remediation

echo "Banner /etc/ssh/banner" >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config
cat > /etc/ssh/banner << 'EOF'
**********************************************************************
 AUTHORIZED ACCESS ONLY
 This system is monitored. All connections are logged.
 Unauthorized access is prohibited and will be prosecuted.
**********************************************************************
EOF
systemctl reload sshd

5.1.6 Ensure sshd Ciphers are configured

STIG: UBTU‑24‑100820 (CAT II)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation · STIG CAT II | Status: ❌ INTENTIONAL DEVIATION (from STIG)

What’s Required - CIS: No weak ciphers (3des‑cbc, aes128‑cbc, aes192‑cbc, aes256‑cbc, arcfour, blowfish‑cbc, cast128‑cbc). - STIG: Only FIPS‑approved ciphers: aes256‑gcm@openssh.com, aes128‑gcm@openssh.com, aes256‑ctr, aes128‑ctr.

Gentoo Implementation The target system uses chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com, aes256-gcm@openssh.com, aes256-ctr (README Part 19.7). ChaCha20‑Poly1305 is not FIPS‑approved but is cryptographically stronger than AES‑128 variants: it is constant‑time on all CPUs, provides better security on machines without AES‑NI, and is recommended by the cryptographic community. This is a deliberate, risk‑informed deviation (see §8).

Audit

sshd -T | grep -i '^ciphers '

5.2 Configure Privilege Escalation — sudo

The sudo utility provides fine‑grained control over privileged command execution. All CIS §5.2 sudo recommendations are satisfied on the target system. The sudo configuration is managed through /etc/sudoers and files in /etc/sudoers.d/; all edits must be performed with visudo to prevent syntax errors.

5.2.3 Log file exists Defaults logfile="/var/log/sudo.log" grep 'logfile' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/* –
5.2.4 Password required (L2) No NOPASSWD tags grep -r 'NOPASSWD' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ –

UBTU‑24‑600130 — Only authorised users in sudo group

STIG: UBTU‑24‑600130 (CAT I)

Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required Only users who require access to security functions may be members of the sudo (or wheel) group.

Gentoo Implementation Only the ahsan user is in the wheel group (README Part 5.6).

Audit

getent group wheel
# Verify only authorised users are listed

5.3 Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)

The PAM stack on the target system is configured in /etc/pam.d/system-auth (README Part 20). Gentoo does not use a PAM configuration manager; the stack files are edited directly. The key modules — pam_faillock, pam_pwquality, pam_pwhistory, and pam_unix — are configured via dedicated configuration files in /etc/security/.

5.3.1.1 Ensure libpam‑pwquality is installed

STIG: UBTU‑24‑100600 (CAT II)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation · STIG CAT II | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

Audit

ls /lib64/security/pam_pwquality.so && echo "✅ installed" || echo "❌ NOT installed"

Remediation

emerge --ask sys-libs/libpwquality
5.3.3.1.1 – 5.3.3.4.4 Quick Reference: All PAM Module Arguments

All PAM arguments are configured via faillock.conf, pwquality.conf, and the PAM stack files (README Part 20). The following table shows the key STIG‑mapped settings:

Setting Configuration File CIS Recommended Value STIG Required Value Gentoo Value Status

unlock_time faillock.conf ≥ 900 or 0 (never) 0 (never) unlock_time = 900 ⚠️ (STIG wants 0)
even_deny_root faillock.conf Level 2 only Required even_deny_root ✅
minlen pwquality.conf ≥ 14 ≥ 15 minlen = 16 ✅ (exceeds both)
difok pwquality.conf ≥ 2 ≥ 8 difok = 8 ✅
dictcheck pwquality.conf 1 1 dictcheck = 1 ✅
enforcing pwquality.conf 1 1 enforcing = 1 ✅

Hash algorithm pam_unix.so sha512 or yescrypt SHA512 yescrypt ✅ (stronger)

grep -v '^#' /etc/security/faillock.conf | grep -v '^$'

grep 'pam_unix.so\|pam_faillock.so\|pam_pwquality.so\|pam_pwhistory.so' /etc/pam.d/system-auth

6. Logging and Auditing

6.1 Configure System Logging — systemd‑journald

The target system uses systemd‑journald as its sole logging system (README Part 6). rsyslog is not installed. Journald is configured for persistent storage with compression and size‑based rotation.

6.1.1.1 Ensure journald service is active

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

Audit

systemctl is-active systemd-journald.service
# Must output: active
6.1.1.2 – 6.1.1.3 Ensure journald log file access and rotation are configured

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required Journal files must have correct permissions (0640), and log rotation must be configured to prevent disk exhaustion.

Gentoo Implementation journald is configured with persistent storage, compression, and size‑based rotation in /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/60-journald.conf (README Part 6).

Audit

grep -E '^(Storage|Compress|SystemMaxUse|MaxFileSec)=' /etc/systemd/journald.conf /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null
6.1.1.4 Ensure only one logging system is in use

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

Audit

systemctl is-active systemd-journald.service
systemctl is-active rsyslog.service 2>/dev/null && echo "⚠️ rsyslog is also running"
STIG Deviation: rsyslog Requirement

STIG: UBTU‑24‑100200, UBTU‑24‑200090

Status: ❌ INTENTIONAL DEVIATION

What the STIG Requires rsyslog must be installed, enabled, and active. Remote access methods must be logged via auth.*, authpriv.*, and daemon.*.

Gentoo Implementation The target system uses systemd‑journald with persistent storage. Journald provides equivalent logging functionality with structured, indexed binary logs. The audit subsystem captures authentication and privilege escalation events (see §6.2). If STIG compliance is legally required, rsyslog can be emerged alongside journald.

Remediation (if STIG compliance is required)

emerge --ask app-admin/rsyslog
systemctl enable --now rsyslog.service

6.2 System Auditing — auditd

The audit subsystem is configured via /etc/audit/auditd.conf (daemon configuration) and /etc/audit/rules.d/99-hardening.rules (ruleset) as described in README Part 15. The comprehensive ruleset covers all CIS §6.2 and STIG audit requirements. On Gentoo, augenrules is enabled via /etc/conf.d/auditd (the USE_AUGENRULES="yes" setting), which merges component rule files from /etc/audit/rules.d/ into /etc/audit/audit.rules at service startup.

6.2.1.1 Ensure auditd packages are installed

All four retention settings are configured in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (README Part 15.2):

Parameter Gentoo Value Description
max_log_file 50 Maximum audit log file size in megabytes
max_log_file_action KEEP_LOGS Do not automatically delete old logs
disk_full_action HALT Halt the system if the audit partition is full
disk_error_action SYSLOG Log a warning if a disk error is detected
space_left_action SYSLOG Warn when disk space is low
admin_space_left_action HALT Halt when administrative space threshold is reached

Status: ✅ COMPLIANT for all retention settings.

Audit

grep -E '^(max_log_file |max_log_file_action |disk_full_action |disk_error_action |space_left_action |admin_space_left_action )' /etc/audit/auditd.conf
6.2.3.1 – 6.2.3.21 Audit Rules

The full audit ruleset is in /etc/audit/rules.d/99-hardening.rules (README Part 15.3). This covers all CIS §6.2.3 and STIG audit rules. Key rule categories include:

Category Rule Key(s) Purpose
File integrity monitoring etc_changes, identity, pam_config, sudoers_change, sshd_config Detect modifications to critical configuration files
Privileged command execution setuid_exec, setgid_exec, sudo_exec, su_exec Log use of setuid/setgid binaries and privilege escalation
Authentication events login_logout, failed_login, session_tracking Track successful and failed authentication attempts
Network socket creation socket_ipv4, socket_ipv6, network_connect Monitor network connections from user processes
Kernel module loading module_load, module_unload, kmod_exec Detect loading and unloading of kernel modules
User/group management user_mgmt_exec, perm_change, owner_change Audit changes to user accounts and file ownership
Time modification time_change, timezone_change Detect changes to system clock and timezone

The ruleset is locked (immutable) via the -e 2 directive after thorough testing.

Status: ✅ COMPLIANT.

Audit

# Count loaded rules
auditctl -l | wc -l

# Verify immutable mode
grep '^-e 2' /etc/audit/rules.d/99-hardening.rules

Remediation (if the rules are not loaded)

augenrules --load
# If immutable mode is active and rules have changed, a reboot is required:
auditctl -s | grep "enabled" | grep -q "2" && echo "Reboot required to load new rules"

6.3 Configure Integrity Checking — AIDE

AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) provides cryptographic file integrity monitoring. It computes SHA‑256 checksums of critical system files and compares them against a known‑good baseline database.

6.3.1 Ensure AIDE is installed

STIG: UBTU‑24‑100100 (CAT II)

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation · STIG CAT II | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

Audit

qpkg -I aide && echo "✅ AIDE installed" || echo "❌ AIDE NOT installed"

Remediation

emerge --ask app-forensics/aide
aide --init
mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db

What’s Required AIDE must run regularly (at least weekly). The database must be updated after legitimate system changes.

Gentoo Implementation A weekly AIDE check is integrated into the weekly-security-scan.timer and its associated script (README Part 18.4.3).

Audit

systemctl list-timers | grep -i aide || \
  grep -r aide /etc/cron* /etc/crontab 2>/dev/null
6.3.3 Ensure cryptographic mechanisms protect audit tools’ integrity

STIG: UBTU‑24‑90890 (CAT II)

Profile: CIS Level 2 – Server & Workstation · STIG CAT II | Status: ⚠️ NEEDS REVIEW

What’s Required AIDE must be configured to use SHA‑512 checksums for all audit tools.

Gentoo Implementation The AIDE configuration must include specific rules for audit tools with sha512. The default AIDE configuration may use sha256; this must be verified or updated.

Audit

grep -E '(/sbin/(audit|au))' /etc/aide/aide.conf 2>/dev/null | grep sha512 || \
  echo "⚠️ SHA-512 not configured for audit tools in AIDE"

Remediation

cat >> /etc/aide/aide.conf << 'EOF'
# Audit Tools — STIG compliance (SHA-512)
/sbin/auditctl    p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
/sbin/auditd      p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
/sbin/ausearch    p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
/sbin/aureport    p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
/sbin/autrace     p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
/sbin/augenrules  p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
EOF
aide --update
mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db

7. System Maintenance

7.1 System File Permissions

All CIS §7.1 file permission recommendations are satisfied on the target system. The following table lists each file and its expected permissions:

File Expected Mode Expected Owner:Group CIS ID
/etc/passwd 0644 root:root 7.1.1
/etc/passwd- 0644 root:root 7.1.2
/etc/group 0644 root:root 7.1.3
/etc/group- 0644 root:root 7.1.4
/etc/shadow 0000 root:root 7.1.5
/etc/shadow- 0000 root:root 7.1.6
/etc/gshadow 0000 root:root 7.1.7
/etc/gshadow- 0000 root:root 7.1.8
/etc/shells 0644 root:root 7.1.9
/etc/security/opasswd 0600 root:root 7.1.10

Status: ✅ COMPLIANT for all files.

Unified Audit

#!/bin/bash
declare -A EXPECTED
EXPECTED=(
    ["/etc/passwd"]="0644:root:root"
    ["/etc/passwd-"]="0644:root:root"
    ["/etc/group"]="0644:root:root"
    ["/etc/group-"]="0644:root:root"
    ["/etc/shadow"]="0000:root:root"
    ["/etc/shadow-"]="0000:root:root"
    ["/etc/gshadow"]="0000:root:root"
    ["/etc/gshadow-"]="0000:root:root"
    ["/etc/shells"]="0644:root:root"
    ["/etc/security/opasswd"]="0600:root:root"
)
for file in "${!EXPECTED[@]}"; do
    if [ -f "$file" ]; then
        IFS=':' read -r exp_perm exp_owner exp_group <<< "${EXPECTED[$file]}"
        actual=$(stat -c '%a:%U:%G' "$file")
        if [[ "$actual" == "$exp_perm:$exp_owner:$exp_group" ]]; then
            echo "✅ $file"
        else
            echo "❌ $file: $actual (expected $exp_perm:$exp_owner:$exp_group)"
        fi
    fi
done

Remediation (for any file with incorrect permissions)

chown root:root <file>
chmod <expected_mode> <file>
7.1.11 – 7.1.13 World‑writable files, unowned files, and SUID/SGID review

Profile: CIS Level 1 – Server & Workstation | Status: ✅ COMPLIANT

What’s Required - No world‑writable files should exist on the local filesystem. - All world‑writable directories must have the sticky bit set. - No files or directories should exist without a valid owner and group. - All SUID and SGID executables must be reviewed and justified.

Gentoo Implementation The system is checked for these conditions as part of regular security scans. Any anomalies are investigated and remediated.

Audit (world‑writable files)

find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 ! -path "/proc/*" ! -path "/sys/*" ! -path "/run/*" 2>/dev/null

Audit (world‑writable directories without sticky bit)

find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000 ! -path "/proc/*" ! -path "/sys/*" 2>/dev/null

Audit (unowned files)

find / -xdev \( -nouser -o -nogroup \) ! -path "/proc/*" ! -path "/sys/*" 2>/dev/null

Audit (SUID/SGID files)

find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) ! -path "/proc/*" ! -path "/sys/*" 2>/dev/null

7.2 Local User and Group Settings

All CIS §7.2 recommendations are satisfied. Key checks:

  • 7.2.1: All accounts in /etc/passwd use shadowed passwords (x in second field).
  • 7.2.2: No empty password fields in /etc/shadow.
  • 7.2.3: All GIDs in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group.
  • 7.2.4–7: No duplicate UIDs, GIDs, usernames, or group names.
  • 7.2.8: All local interactive user home directories exist, are owned by the user, and have mode 0750 or more restrictive.
  • 7.2.9: User dot files (.forward, .rhost, .netrc, .bash_history) have correct permissions.

Status: ✅ COMPLIANT for all checks.

Unified Audit (key checks)

# 7.2.1 - Shadowed passwords
awk -F: '($2 != "x") {print "User: " $1 " not shadowed"}' /etc/passwd

# 7.2.2 - Empty passwords
awk -F: '($2 == "") {print $1 " has empty password"}' /etc/shadow

# 7.2.4 - Duplicate UIDs
cut -f3 -d: /etc/passwd | sort -n | uniq -d | while read uid; do
    echo "Duplicate UID $uid: $(awk -F: -v u=$uid '$3==u{print $1}' /etc/passwd | xargs)"
done

# 7.2.5 - Duplicate GIDs
cut -f3 -d: /etc/group | sort -n | uniq -d | while read gid; do
    echo "Duplicate GID $gid: $(awk -F: -v g=$gid '$3==g{print $1}' /etc/group | xargs)"
done

8. Cryptographic Requirements

The target system’s cryptographic choices are optimised for the APT (Advanced Persistent Threat) threat model rather than for FIPS compliance. The following table documents each intentional deviation:

Cryptographic Use Gentoo Choice FIPS‑Approved Equivalent Rationale
LUKS key derivation Argon2id (1 GiB memory cost) PBKDF2 Argon2id is memory‑hard; resists GPU/ASIC brute‑force
Password hashing (PAM) yescrypt SHA‑512 yescrypt is memory‑hard; recommended by systemd upstream
SSH encryption ChaCha20‑Poly1305 AES‑128‑GCM Constant‑time on all CPUs; no AES‑NI dependency
SSH key exchange sntrup761x25519‑sha512, mlkem768x25519‑sha256 ECDH NIST P‑256/384/521 Post‑quantum hybrid; quantum‑safe

FIPS mode (fips=1 on the kernel command line) is not enabled. FIPS is a compliance standard, not a security standard. Enabling it would require downgrading several cryptographic choices, weakening the system against the nation‑state APT threat model.

UBTU‑24‑600030 — FIPS 140‑3 mode must be enabled

STIG: UBTU‑24‑600030 (CAT I)

Status: ❌ INTENTIONAL DEVIATION

What the STIG Requires The system must run in FIPS mode and use only FIPS‑validated cryptographic modules.

Gentoo Implementation FIPS mode is not enabled. See rationale above.

Remediation (if FIPS compliance is legally required)

# Add fips=1 to /etc/kernel/cmdline and rebuild UKI
# Rebuild LUKS with: cryptsetup luksFormat --pbkdf pbkdf2 ...
# Replace yescrypt with sha512 in PAM
# Remove ChaCha20 and post‑quantum algorithms from SSH
# Enable 'fips' USE flag globally and rebuild @world

What’s Required All persistent disk partitions must be encrypted at
